title: Perturbations, state, and sampling paths
subtitle: SOMA · Scheduler tensor aliasing · Data breadth · DDIM
intro: Two main readings and three briefs separate perturbation guarantees, implementation state, and data composition. The DDIM classic examines how one training objective permits different sampling paths.

articles.authors: Geetika · Shivani Singh Chauhan · Gauranshi Gupta · Anant Jain · Kaushik Kalyanaraman · Bapi Chatterjee
articles.title: Stale perturbations: what convergence survives?
articles.evidence: Read Algorithm 1, §§4–5 and Theorem 1; not reproduced

blocks.text: SAM (2021) usually needs two gradient evaluations per step. SOMA transforms a stale gradient residual after subtracting a momentum-based EMA. Indices below follow Algorithm 1; NS denotes a finite-step spectral transform.[1]

blocks.label: ρ is the perturbation scale; γ is the residual coefficient; initialization is separate [1]
Original update: T+1 gradient evaluations over T steps, versus 2T for FP-SOMA [1]

blocks.text: Theorem 1 assumes a lower-bounded objective, operator/nuclear-norm Hölder smoothness and bounded p-th central noise moments with independent minibatches. It controls the average expected nuclear gradient norm, retaining a floor proportional to ρ raised to ν. Direction-insensitivity of this bound does not establish better generalization.[1]

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Fewer gradient evaluations do not imply proportional wall-clock savings. Appendix proofs and LLM experiments were not fully checked; no performance gain is asserted here.[1]

articles.paper: Taming Orthogonal Optimizers at Scale (Part 2): The Anatomy of a Silent Tensor-Aliasing Bug
articles.title: When the scheduler changes the experiment
articles.dateNote: Public on 2026-10-25; linked by the author’s same-day forum post
articles.evidence: Read reproduction, fix and recovery-test descriptions; code not executed

blocks.text: In this OLMo-core/Dion3 integration, lr and initial_lr referenced the same scalar tensor. An in-place scheduler update therefore changed its own baseline. Converting values during checkpoint serialization preserved an already corrupted baseline.[2,3]

blocks.label: Illustrative recurrence assuming each step multiplies an overwritten baseline; not a universal scheduler theorem

blocks.text: The fix registers initial_lr using float(lr), separating the immutable baseline from the runtime tensor. The author reports matching learning-rate trajectories for 20 uninterrupted steps versus a cold restart after step 10, plus HSDP/FP8 interruption checks.[2]

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Short runs and author-reported checks establish neither long-run optimizer superiority nor correctness of every checkpoint path. The direct evidence concerns learning-rate recovery.[2]

articles.paper: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
articles.title: Capability depends on the training mixture
articles.dateNote: Released in the October 23–24 window; original page has no precise displayed date; catch-up
articles.evidence: Read training overview and data-removal comparison; internal evaluation not independently reproduced

blocks.text: The original blog reports internal xdev-bench-hard pass@3 falling from 90.5% to 81.0% after removing cyber data from mid-training and related RL environments. This is not pass@1. Both stages changed together, preventing separate attribution; no fitted compute–performance curve is provided. The technical comparison, rather than the launch itself, is included.[4]

articles.paper: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
articles.title: Selection can dominate long-context training

blocks.text: HyTopK finds exact top-k indices online; selection replay reuses them during recomputation. The paper reports 2.07× end-to-end GLM-5.1 training speedup over Megatron-LM at 1M context on 512 H20 GPUs. Layer-level gains for other architectures are not whole-model gains. This studies context-dependent compute costs, not a new loss scaling law.[5]

articles.paper: POSEIDON: Scaling Training Environments for Scientific Agents from Code Repositories
articles.title: Expand source diversity at a fixed trajectory budget
articles.evidence: Read §4.3 ablations; other experiments not fully checked

blocks.text: For Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, repository coverage rises from 20% to 100% at fixed trajectory count, average difficulty and task proportions: four benchmarks improve overall, with intermediate fluctuations. At 30,000 trajectories, raising mean difficulty from 2.4 to 3.2 gives no consistent benefit. These ablations distinguish source breadth from difficulty; they establish no universal power law.[6]

classic.authors: Jiaming Song · Chenlin Meng · Stefano Ermon
classic.title: A training objective does not uniquely determine the sampler
classic.evidence: Read §§3–5, Theorem 1 and Table 1; not reproduced
classic.question: How can reward drift be controlled when changing samplers?

blocks.text: DDPM (2020) training uses noisy marginals without uniquely fixing path coupling. DDIM (ICLR 2021) changes that coupling, reusing one denoiser across samplers.[7,8]

blocks.label: α is cumulative retained signal, decreasing with t; not a one-step coefficient [7]
Theorem 1: path-dependent variational objectives equal weighted denoising losses plus a θ-independent constant [7]

blocks.text: Weight-independent optima require unshared parameters across times; finite shared networks retain trade-offs. Deterministic sampling takes the zero-noise limit.[7]

blocks.label: Original sampler extended to s<t; z is independent standard Gaussian [7]
η controls stochasticity; a sparse time grid reduces denoiser calls [7]

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Equal training objectives do not ensure equal finite-step output distributions. Table 1 reports CelebA FID 13.73 for 20-step DDIM, a setting-specific result. Question: how can fine-tuning constrain reward drift after switching samplers?[7]
